rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses appears more than any other prophet in the Qur’an, and this account is chiefly a spiritual example rather than history.
rows.anchor: Moses is featured more prominently than any other prophet in the Quran. Here his account is given more as a spiritual example than as history

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story also allegorizes some of Muhammad’s challenges and connects to other accounts of Moses’ mission.
rows.anchor: serves as an allegory for some of the Prophet Muhammad’s own challenges

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Ṭs
rows.claim: “Our signs” means proofs and evidence.
rows.anchor: Our signs, meaning with proofs and evidence (Ṭ, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is verbatim in 11:96; the wording also appears in 14:5 and 43:46, while 23:45 sends Moses and Aaron with signs.
rows.anchor: This verse is found verbatim in 11:96

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: The signs can specifically refer to the nine clear signs in 17:101, cf. 27:12.
rows.anchor: Our signs can be read as a reference to the nine clear signs mentioned in 17:101 (cf. 27:12; Q)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: A manifest authority can refer to the Torah.
rows.anchor: A manifest authority means a clear proof and is understood as a reference to the Torah (Q)

rows.speaker: Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: Alternatively, it refers to Moses’ miracles.
rows.anchor: or to the miracles that Moses performed (Ṭs, Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hāmān was a Pharaoh’s-court member, probably head of the quarries, ordered to build a tower.
rows.anchor: Hāmān was a member of Pharaoh’s court, most likely the head of his quarries, who was ordered to light a fire and make me a tower

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Korah was a wealthy court member and grandson of Levi who was swallowed by the ground for opposing Moses.
rows.anchor: Korah, another member of Pharaoh’s court and a grandson of Levi (Numbers 16:21), had vast wealth, but was swallowed by the ground for opposing Moses (Numbers 16:41)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The trio called Moses a sorcerer, as Quraysh later accused Muhammad; the charge appears elsewhere in the cited verses.
rows.anchor: The reaction of Pharaoh, Hāmān, and Korah to the signs and the manifest authority was to accuse Moses of being a sorcerer

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s second order aimed to humiliate the Israelites, reduce their numbers, or both; the first sought to prevent a prophet like Moses from arising.
rows.anchor: the first was to eliminate the possibility of a prophet such as Moses arising among them; the second was to humiliate them, to reduce their numbers, or both (IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In 7:127 the order appears to be collective punishment for following Moses.
rows.anchor: In 7:127 it appears to be a form of collective punishment for following Moses

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Ṭs
rows.claim: The women were kept alive as servants, not out of mercy, which further humiliated the Israelites.
rows.anchor: The women were not spared out of mercy, but so that they could continue to live as servants (Ṭ), which was a further humiliation (Ṭ, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Some say God distracted Pharaoh and his people from carrying out the order by sending a plague.
rows.anchor: According to some, God distracted Pharaoh and his people from carrying out this punishment by sending the plague upon them (Q)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: On that view, the phrase refers to the failure of Pharaoh’s plan.
rows.anchor: the scheming of the disbelievers is naught but astray can be understood as a reference to the failure of Pharaoh’s plan (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators do not say whether the second order was carried out.
rows.anchor: Most commentators do not say whether the plan was carried out

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī, who elsewhere says the order was carried out, reads this more generally: disbelievers’ schemes eventually fail.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī, who says elsewhere that it was (see 7:127c), interprets the scheming of the disbelievers is naught but astray as a more general reference to the schemes of all disbelievers eventually coming to naught

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It may also recall that the first order failed because Moses survived, and that the renewed order would fail too.
rows.anchor: the first time Pharaoh ordered that the sons of the Israelites be slain, the plan failed, since Moses was spared; so this time it would fail again

rows.speaker: IJ, Ṭs
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s “Leave me” implies that some retinue members feared Moses and warned against killing him, sensing he would destroy them.
rows.anchor: among Pharaoh’s retinue were some who feared Moses and warned against killing him, sensing that Moses would bring destruction upon them (IJ, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: IJ, Ṭs
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s professed fear of changed religion means fear Moses would turn people from worshipping Pharaoh and believing in his divinity.
rows.anchor: turn them away from their worship of Pharaoh himself (IJ) and their belief in his divinity(Ṭs)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The corruption charge echoes Pharaoh’s notables in 7:127.
rows.anchor: The accusation that Moses will cause corruption to appear in the land reflects the question posed to Pharaoh by his notables in 7:127

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses responds to Pharaoh’s threat by seeking refuge in God.
rows.anchor: Moses’ response is then to seek refuge in God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those spreading corruption present themselves as righteous and opponents as corrupt, as in 2:11; 30:41 is cited for the broader theme.
rows.anchor: those who work corruption cast themselves as the righteous and their opponents as the corrupt, as in 2:11

rows.speaker: IJ, IK, Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: Many identify the believing man as Pharaoh’s cousin.
rows.anchor: Many propose that he was a cousin of Pharaoh (IJ, IK, Q, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: IJ, Ṭ
rows.claim: Others say he was an Israelite, reading the phrase as a believer concealing his faith from Pharaoh’s family.
rows.anchor: Others say that he was an Israelite, in which case the meaning of this opening phrase is understood to be “a believing man who was concealing his belief from the family of Pharaoh” (IJ, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī argues he was from Pharaoh’s family because a court outsider would not have been heard.
rows.anchor: Al-Ṭabarī argues that he was a man from Pharaoh’s family, since if he had been an Israelite or another person outside of Pharaoh’s court, no one in the court would have listened to him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In either account, he is the man in 28:20 who ran to warn Moses that the notables plotted against him.
rows.anchor: In either interpretation, the believing man is the same person to whom reference is made in 28:20

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His protest resembles the sorcerers’ complaint after Pharaoh sentenced them for believing Moses; 5:59 and 85:9 condemn vengeance over belief.
rows.anchor: The question, Will you kill a man for saying, “My Lord is God”? is similar to the sorcerers’ complaint to Pharaoh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believer argues that truthful speech, especially backed by evidentiary miracles, cannot merit punishment.
rows.anchor: if Moses is truthful, he cannot be punished for speaking the truth, especially since he has brought clear proofs in the form of evidentiary miracles

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Moses lies, he bears the consequences of his lie, so there is no need to punish him.
rows.anchor: if he is a liar, he will suffer the consequences of his lies; so there is no need to punish him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Punishing Moses if he is truthful will bring even greater afflictions on his punishers.
rows.anchor: if he is punished for telling the truth, then even greater afflictions will befall those who punish him

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Here “prodigal” can mean “idolater.”

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: It can also mean one who transgresses God’s limits by lying about God.
rows.anchor: or one who transgresses the limits set by God by lying about God (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: “The land” is Egypt; their sovereignty indicates Egyptian power over Israelites.
rows.anchor: The land refers to Egypt. That the Egyptians have sovereignty over it and prevail over it indicates their power over the Israelites (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭs
rows.claim: Some understand the believer to urge gratitude for their powerful position.
rows.anchor: Some understand the believing man to be enjoining them to have gratitude for their position of power (IK, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He uses their worldly power to argue they must recognize Moses’ God, since no one else can protect them from divine punishment.
rows.anchor: he is also using their unsurpassed power to argue that they must recognize the God of Moses, since there is no one other than themselves to protect them against punishment from Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh avoids the believer’s argument and relies on his authority.
rows.anchor: instead relying upon his authority

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: The phrase may mean Pharaoh indicates only what he thinks right or teaches only what he knows.
rows.anchor: I do not indicate to you anything other than what I believe to be right,” or “I do not teach you anything other than what I know” (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Ibn Kathīr
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr says Pharaoh’s claim is a lie because 27:14 says he and his people inwardly knew the signs’ truth.
rows.anchor: Ibn Kathīr argues that in the context of other verses pertaining to the story of Moses, this statement is a lie, since 27:14 says

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: For Pharaoh, rectitude meant denying and killing Moses and treating Pharaoh as a god.
rows.anchor: In Pharaoh’s view the way of rectitude means denying and killing Moses and taking Pharaoh as a god (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh led his people astray (20:79), and they followed an unsound command (11:97).
rows.anchor: Thus Pharaoh led his people astray, and guided them not (20:79). Nonetheless, they followed the command of Pharaoh, and the command of Pharaoh was not sound (11:97)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: “Parties” are groups that joined forces against a prophet.
rows.anchor: Parties [of old] refers to those who joined forces to make common cause against a prophet (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: The day is when each group faced God’s punishment with no protector.
rows.anchor: The day of the parties [of old] refers to the day that each of them eventually faced when God’s Punishment came upon them and they had no one to protect them (IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿĀd and Thamūd were pre-Islamic Arabian tribes that rejected their prophets; the commentary cites their accounts.
rows.anchor: The ʿĀd and the Thamūd are pre-Islamic Arabian tribes that rejected the prophets sent to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This resembles Qur’anic warnings to disbelievers, but here the warning comes from a believer rather than a prophet.
rows.anchor: This warning is akin to similar warnings issued to the disbelievers throughout the Quran, though it differs in that a prophet does not issue it

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: God’s destruction of the past peoples was just and equitable.
rows.anchor: indicates that God’s destruction of them was just and equitable (Z)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: The phrase also says God does not desire worldly injustice, central to Shiite and Muʿtazilite Divine Justice.
rows.anchor: God does not desire the wrong or injustice that occurs in the world (Ṭs), a position that is central to both the Shiite and the Muʿtazilite understanding of Divine Justice

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Resurrection is named for exchanges between Garden and Fire inhabitants, hypocrites calling believers, and angels announcing the Garden (7:43–44, 50; 57:13–14).
rows.anchor: the Day of Resurrection is referred to as the Day of Mutual Calling, because the inhabitants of the Garden will call out to the inhabitants of the Fire

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On that day disbelievers flee from the Fire and one another, as in 80:34–36.
rows.anchor: The disbelievers will turn away to flee from the Fire, but they will also flee from one another

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an says those God leads astray have no way, guide, or protector (4:88,143; 42:46; 7:186; 13:33; 39:23,36; 18:17; 42:44; cf. 10:27).
rows.anchor: For those whom God leads astray the Quran says there is no way (4:88, 143; 42:46), no guide (7:186; 13:33; 39:23, 36), and no protector (18:17; 42:44); cf. 10:27

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: Some take Joseph’s proofs as his argument that the One God is better than many lords and idols lack authority.
rows.anchor: clear proofs refers to Joseph’s rhetorical argument in 12:39–40

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: Others take them to be Joseph’s evidentiary miracles.
rows.anchor: Others say that clear proofs refers to Joseph’s evidentiary miracles (R, Z)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Another view identifies the proofs as Joseph’s visions and dream interpretation.
rows.anchor: or his visions and his corresponding ability to interpret dreams (Q)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: People accepted Joseph’s worldly judgment due to his high Egyptian office, but not his religious claims.
rows.anchor: the people were willing to follow Joseph’s judgment in worldly matters related to his high position in the Egyptian government, but not with regard to religious matters (IK)

rows.speaker: IK, R
rows.claim: Their claim expressed their wish and showed rejection of prophethood.
rows.anchor: Their saying, God will not send a messenger after him, would then express their wish and demonstrate their disbelief in and rejection of prophethood (IK, R)

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī sees this as an instance of God turning disbelievers from truth and its path.
rows.anchor: According to al-Ṭabarī, this is among the ways in which God turns disbelievers away from attaining the truth and following the way

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is the second of four rebukes in the sūrah against disputing God’s signs; the others are 40:4, 56, and 69.
rows.anchor: This is the second of four verses in this sūrah to rebuke those who dispute concerning God’s signs; also see vv. 4, 56, and 69

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Disputing without authority means arguing without proof or relying on blind imitation and base sophisms.
rows.anchor: To dispute without authority (cf. v. 56) means to argue without proof

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s seal closes people’s ability to understand; the commentary cites other Qur’anic occurrences.
rows.anchor: God’s sealing hearts indicates that He has closed their ability to understand

rows.speaker: Q, R, Ṭ
rows.claim: The phrase may instead be read “every arrogant tyrannical heart.”
rows.anchor: The heart of every arrogant tyrant can also be read, “every arrogant tyrannical heart” (Q, R,Ṭ)

rows.speaker: al-Qurṭubī
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī prefers the alternative because arrogance begins in the heart before the other faculties follow.
rows.anchor: as al-Qurṭubī observes, it is the heart that first becomes arrogant and then the rest of one’s faculties follow

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet says the heart is a lump of flesh; its soundness or corruption determines the soundness or corruption of the whole body. No grading is stated.
rows.anchor: the famous saying of the Prophet, “In the body there is a lump of flesh. When it is sound, the entire body is sound

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh exemplifies the arrogant tyrant whose sealed heart disputes God’s signs and even God’s existence.
rows.anchor: Pharaoh’s response provides an illustration of the manner in which the heart of an arrogant tyrant is sealed

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Some say Pharaoh feared the believer’s argument might enter his people’s hearts.
rows.anchor: Some interpret Pharaoh’s response to mean that he feared that the words of the believing man would enter into the hearts of his people (Q)

rows.speaker: IK, Q, Ṭ, Ṭs
rows.claim: The expression usually means paths or doors to heaven, or means by which one attains what one seeks.
rows.anchor: which is usually understood to mean “paths to the heavens” (IK, Q, Ṭ, Ṭs), “doors to the heavens” (IK, Q, Ṭ, Ṭs), or those things by means of which one can attain what one seeks

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s wish to see God shows he mistakenly imagines God as a physical being in a place.
rows.anchor: Pharaoh’s desire to look upon the God of Moses demonstrates his complete misunderstanding, in that he takes God to be a physical being occupying a particular space (Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This contrasts with Moses’ request at Sinai and repentance when he could not endure the vision (7:143).
rows.anchor: It also provides a notable contrast to Moses’ request to God on Mt. Sinai, My Lord, show me, that I might look upon Thee (7:143)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The corrupt are often deluded by Satan, ultimately by God, into thinking their conduct good; Pharaoh’s council may also have reinforced this.
rows.anchor: Those who are corrupt are often portrayed as deluded, sometimes by Satan (see 8:48; 16:63; 27:24; 29:38), but ultimately by God (see 27:4)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s council may have made his conduct seem fair.
rows.anchor: Here it may also have been Pharaoh’s council of notables that made the evil of his conduct seem fair unto him (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭs
rows.claim: The wording may mean God turned Pharaoh aside, or that Pharaoh turned himself away and blocked others from the right path.
rows.anchor: a phrase that could also be read, “and he turned from the way,” meaning that he turned himself away and that he prevented others from following the right way (Q, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believer promises the very way Pharaoh claimed to guide them to in 40:29.
rows.anchor: The way of rectitude is what Pharaoh promised to guide the people to in v. 29

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording translates sabīl al-rashād and resembles sabīl al-rushd, “the way of sound judgment” in 7:146.
rows.anchor: which is similar to the way of sound judgment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description of arrogant people in 7:146 fits Pharaoh and his notables.
rows.anchor: The latter phrase aptly describes the case of Pharaoh and his notables

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh and his notables rejected the arguments and continued to deny the divine origin of the miracles.
rows.anchor: who were presented not only with the arguments posed here and elsewhere, but also with evidentiary miracles whose Divine Origin they continued to deny

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an repeatedly contrasts this world’s delusive delights with the Hereafter, which is “life indeed.”
rows.anchor: This is one of several verses to affirm that the ephemeral delights of this world are naught but the enjoyment of delusion

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: A hadith transmitted by ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd compares the Prophet and this world to a rider briefly resting in a tree’s shade before moving on; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: transmitted by ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd states, “The Messenger of God was lying down

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God shows mercy and bounty, requiting evil only with its like and not wronging anyone even by a mote’s weight.
rows.anchor: God shows mercy and bounty in judging human actions, but requites evil deeds with nothing but their like

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī calls this a principle of Islamic law: punishment must never exceed the crime.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī notes that this is also a fundamental principle in Islamic Law, according to which the punishment must never exceed the crime

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God multiplies good deeds tenfold or seven hundredfold; other verses say good deeds bring what is better.
rows.anchor: He multiplies good deeds ten times the like thereof (6:160) or even seven hundred fold (see 2:261)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Spiritual potential and reward do not depend on gender; 33:35 especially affirms equal reward for religious observance.
rows.anchor: Such rewards relate to the human condition irrespective of gender

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: One view takes “without reckoning” to mean that Paradise’s rewards are endless.
rows.anchor: Without reckoning could be understood as a reference to the rewards of Paradise being without end (R)

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: Another view says bad deeds require reckoning while good deeds do not.
rows.anchor: the recompense for bad deeds requires a reckoning, while the recompense for good deeds does not (R, Z)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: A further view says faith enables entry without reckoning, since recompense based only on deeds would require reckoning.
rows.anchor: were people to be recompensed in accord with their deeds alone, there would be a reckoning (Ṭs), implying that it is their faith and belief that allow them to enter the Garden without reckoning

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The believer asks why they call him to the Fire when he calls them to belief and salvation.
rows.anchor: This verse means, “How is it that when I call you to belief, which leads to salvation, you call me to disbelief, which leads to the Fire?” (R)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: The idolaters’ claims have no verification in revelation or reason.
rows.anchor: That whereof I have no knowledge indicates that there is nothing in revelation or reason that would verify the disbelievers’ claims (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Pairing “the Mighty” with “the Forgiving” joins apparently disparate Divine Attributes, as in 40:3.
rows.anchor: The combination of the Divine Names the Mighty and the Forgiving (cf. 39:5; 38:66; 67:2) expresses the manner in which God brings together all of the seemingly disparate Divine Attributes (Aj), as in v. 3

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A more frequent pairing is “the Mighty and the Merciful,” found in the cited verses.
rows.anchor: This is similar to the more frequent combination of the Names the Mighty and the Merciful

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ, R
rows.claim: Idols cannot intercede, harm or benefit worshippers, or answer their pleas.
rows.anchor: the idols’ inability to intercede on behalf of those who worship them, in this life or the next (Q), harm or benefit them (Ṭ), or respond to their pleas (R)

rows.speaker: Aj, R, Z
rows.claim: Alternatively, idols themselves do not call their worshippers even if idolaters call people to worship them; both senses can coexist.
rows.anchor: although the idolaters call people to worship the idols, the idols themselves do not call them (Aj, R, Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both interpretations appear in 46:5–6: the idols do not answer and will later disavow worshippers.
rows.anchor: Both meanings can be present at the same time, as in 46:5–6

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary refers to its note on the Qur’anic use of “prodigal.”
rows.anchor: For the Quranic usage of prodigal, see 10:12c

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: The warning says punishment will come, and the disbelievers will learn the truth too late for it to help them.
rows.anchor: the punishment of which he speaks will come upon the disbelievers and they will know the truth of what he enjoined, but then it will be too late

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The words may foreshadow Pharaoh’s belated testimony as the sea closes over him.
rows.anchor: the verse may foretell Pharaoh’s belated testimony, uttered when the sea closes in upon him

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: The believer may fear Pharaoh and the followers who intend to kill him.
rows.anchor: I entrust my affair to God could indicate that the man feared Pharaoh and that his followers intended to kill him (Q, R)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The believer’s words echo Moses’ response to Pharaoh’s threat in 40:27.
rows.anchor: In this way, it reflects the response of Moses to Pharaoh’s threat to kill him

rows.speaker: Aj, Bq, Su
rows.claim: Entrusting oneself to God precedes the divine decree; submitting oneself follows it.
rows.anchor: oneself to God follows it (Aj, Bq, Su)

rows.speaker: Dhu’l-Nūn al-Miṣrī
rows.claim: Dhu’l-Nūn says entrusting means despairing of one’s actions and soul, taking refuge in God in every state, and attaching oneself only to God.
rows.anchor: The famous Egyptian Sufi Dhu’l-Nūn al-Miṣrī

rows.speaker: Rūzbihān al-Baqlī
rows.claim: Perfect entrusting means seeing no independent power to benefit or harm and seeing God in every breath.
rows.anchor: According to the Persian Sufi Rūzbihān al-Baqlī, “The perfection of entrusting is to not see oneself or anything else as having any power to benefit or harm

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: God knows His servants’ states and needs in all their affairs.
rows.anchor: God sees His servants in all of their affairs, knowing their states and their needs at all times (R)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: For his faith and affirmation of Moses, God protected the believer from Pharaoh’s people.
rows.anchor: For his faith and his affirming Moses, God protected the believing man from Pharaoh’s people (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plot may mean Pharaoh’s severe punishments for opponents, including the sorcerers’ threatened mutilation and crucifixion.
rows.anchor: That which they had plotted may refer to the severe punishments Pharaoh was known to inflict upon those who opposed him

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: The believer’s escape from punishment may result from entrusting his affair to God.
rows.anchor: His being spared such punishment can be seen as a result of his entrusting his affair to God (Aj)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The punishment most likely refers to Pharaoh and his people drowning while pursuing Moses and the Israelites.
rows.anchor: the punishment that encompassed Pharaoh and his people most likely refers to their drowning in the sea as they pursued Moses and the Israelites

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ḥāqaba literally means “enclosed,” alluding to punishment that overtakes plotters and those who mocked.
rows.anchor: more literally, “enclosed,” alludes to the punishment resulting from their own plotting
